title: Seeing it is seeing
hookLine: whoever sees dependent origination sees the dhamma (MN 28)
carry: the seeing is the real thing

cards: A monk named Vakkali lies gravely ill in a potter's shed. Tradition says he had loved the Buddha so much that he followed him around just to look at his face.
Now the Buddha comes to his bedside, and Vakkali stirs, trying to get up. For a long time, he says, he'd wanted to come and see the Blessed One, but his body hadn't let him.
The Buddha's answer turns what seeing means inside out.

teach.h: WHOEVER SEES THE DHAMMA SEES ME.
teach.b: Here's what the Buddha told Vakkali, in the Connected Discourses. Enough, Vakkali. Why do you want to see this rotting body?
Whoever sees the Dhamma sees me; whoever sees me sees the Dhamma. It isn't cold. It's a gift: you don't need my face; you need what I've been pointing at.
Now go back to the very first day of this block, the elephant's footprint, Sariputta's great talk in the Middle-Length Discourses.
Near its end, after walking through the body's elements and the five heaps, Sariputta quotes the Buddha with a line of the same shape. Whoever sees dependent origination sees the Dhamma.
Whoever sees the Dhamma sees dependent origination. Put the two together. To see the Buddha is to see the Dhamma.

To see the Dhamma is to see dependent arising: this, because of that. So in these two suttas, the seeing that counts isn't of a person or a place or a vision. It's seeing how things lean on each other.
How a mood leans on sleep. How craving leans on feeling. How dukkha leans on craving, and ends when craving ends.
Sariputta draws the conclusion right there in the sutta: the five heaps are dependently arisen, and the desire and clinging for them is the origin of dukkha.

teach.h: THE SEEING IS THE REAL THING.
teach.b: Seeing it isn't a step before the real thing.
The seeing is the real thing.

how: Buddhist teachers often pair the line from MN 28 with the Buddha's words to Vakkali to explain that the teaching, not the teacher's body, is what students are meant to see.

o: the teaching, and the way things are
a holy relic kept in a temple
a rule book for monks and nuns

games.q: match each line to who said or heard it.
p: wanted to see the Buddha's body

s: the Buddha told Vakkali to keep gazing at him
he said: why see this body? whoever sees the Dhamma sees me.
MN 28, the elephant's footprint, contains the line about dependent origination
Sariputta quotes it near the end of the talk.
in MN 28, seeing the Dhamma means having a vision of light
it means seeing dependent arising: how things lean on each other.

games.q: you're the Buddha, at the bedside of a sick monk who has always longed to look at you. he tries to get up to see you. what do you say?
o: stay and look at me as long as you like.
why see this body? whoever sees the Dhamma sees me.
you must get well before you see me.
games.why: the Buddha turned Vakkali's eyes from his body to the teaching: whoever sees the Dhamma sees me.

practice: Choose one small thing happening in you right now, a sound, an ache, a thought, and ask what it depends on: the sound on the ear, the air, the source; the ache on how you're sitting.
Stay with just one link until you can see it plainly, without commentary. Then rest, and let the seeing be enough.

wordCard.voice: Dhamma. The teaching, and the way things are: whoever sees dependent arising sees the dhamma, and whoever sees the dhamma sees the Buddha.

orig.note: Pali dhamma, Sanskrit dharma: the teaching, and the way things are, which the teaching points to.

carryVoice: Your line: the seeing is the real thing. Understanding why something happened is already a kind of seeing. Day three hundred fifty-one, done.

sources.ref: MN 28 (Mahahatthipadopama Sutta), the line on dependent origination
